item.title: Legal Sports Betting in NC Will Bring Revenue and Ethical Challenges. It Could Also Set the Stage for a Cheating Scandal
item.description:
Legal Sports Betting in NC Will Bring Revenue and Ethical Challenges. It Could Also Set the Stage for a Cheating Scandal vabreese@david… Tue, 06/13/2023 - 14:24

Legal Sports Betting in NC Will Bring Revenue and Ethical Challenges. It Could Also Set the Stage for a Cheating Scandal

1709726400

Legal online sports betting promises a windfall for the state of North Carolina and sportsbooks, but it could also create a slew of unintended consequences. 

Sean McKeever, Professor of Philosophy

Online sports betting will be available to North Carolinians on Monday, March 11. Estimates indicate the state would take in $71 million annually by mid-2028 with much of that money supporting local, regional and state athletics initiatives, athletic programs at most University of North Carolina system schools, and problem-gambling programs.

But legal gambling also brings a host of ethical challenges. We asked Professor of Philosophy Sean McKeever about how widespread gambling could affect the integrity of professional and amateur sports. McKeever regularly teaches a “Philosophy of Sport” class where students explore sports ethics in detail.

How does an ethicist examine gambling—something most people consider unethical?

Well, some people think gambling is a vice pure and simple, but unless one can spell out why it is a vice, this can seem like undue moralizing. Others think gambling ought to be forbidden because gamblers harm themselves. 

Talking about gambling this way quickly becomes a classic argument that pits paternalism against freedom. If we are not harming others, shouldn’t we be free to dispose of our money as we see fit? We do not generally forbid people from making foolish financial decisions. 

Finally, some people think gambling is wrong because it has widespread harmful effects on society, like encouraging debt, or greed, or crime. If this is the argument, then it is important not just to assume that gambling has those effects. One needs to look carefully at the evidence.

However, I think one thing is clear: We shouldn’t lump all gambling together; some forms of gambling might pose different threats than others.

What makes betting on sports different from other casino games?

What strikes me as potentially distinctive about sports gambling is that sports (unlike most other forms of gambling) have a real value outside of gambling. No one would play poker or take guesses at the roulette wheel unless doing so was a way of resolving a bet. 

But we could very well have basketball, soccer, tennis, football and so on without gambling. 

So, sports gambling is special because it presents a threat to an otherwise valuable human activity. 

So, sports gambling requires special consideration because it affects something many Americans enjoy? 

The stakes are really high. They fear that the spread of sports betting will damage their leagues, which are built on the premise of fair play. 

And if that is a concern, it is important to be concrete and realistic. We should avoid high-minded but ultimately empty tsk-tsk-ing. If Davidson plays an A10 tournament game, nothing is tainted merely because someone puts a bet on it. However, history teaches that the money behind gambling has interests of its own and that can lead to corruption like the infamous 1919 “Black Sox” scandal. The question to ask, and I am agnostic about the answer, is how much risk of corruption does gambling create?

What would happen if widespread legal gambling began to affect the outcomes of games?

The consequences are huge. The NCAA basketball tournament would not generate more than a billion dollars in revenue if fans thought — or even strongly suspected — that the games were fixed. And beyond money, almost every devoted athlete cares deeply that games are won or lost on the basis of fair play and athletic skill. If that ceased to be the case, I think most athletes would feel that what they most love about sport had been lost.

In addition, the dawn of NIL (name, image, likeness) in college sports is likely to create a situation where some players on some teams are earning significant NIL income while other players earn little or nothing. I fear that pairing that income disparity with sports betting may create exactly the environment in which a cheating scandal is likely.

Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has sparked outrage and an outpouring of support for Ukraine’s citizens from around the world.

Davidson College and surrounding communities continue to organize events and curate resources in an effort to aid Ukrainians, raise awareness of the crisis and educate those who want to know more about Russia, Ukraine and the historical and cultural context around this unprovoked conflict. 

This page is a non-exhaustive list of the resources and events being organized on campus and nearby. We will continue to update this as new information and opportunities to show support for Ukraine become available.

Leave a note (or photo or postcard) on the Fishbowl walls to show support or share a remembrance.

item.title: Holocaust History Focal Point of Davidson Basketball Trip to Berlin
item.description:
Holocaust History Focal Point of Davidson Basketball Trip to Berlin vabreese@david… Mon, 09/28/2026 - 14:27

Holocaust History Focal Point of Davidson Basketball Trip to Berlin

Davidson Men's Basketball team visiting the Sachsenhausen Memorial and Museum in Germany.

1790596800

Over four days in August, the Davidson College men's basketball team traveled through Berlin to gain a deeper understanding of the Nazis’ rise to power and the roots of the Holocaust.

They traveled with the Benjamin Ferencz Institute for Ethics, Human Rights and the Holocaust, a nonprofit focused on Holocaust education and remembrance that is named for the Nuremberg prosecutor who tried Nazi officers for crimes against humanity. (Ferencz Institute Founding Director Stacy Gallin recently reflected on the trip in an op-ed in the Times of Israel.)

The Wildcats’ itinerary took them to the Olympic Stadium the Nazi regime built to sell itself to the world. They walked the grounds of the Wannsee Villa, where officials gathered around a table in 1942 to coordinate the murder of Europe's Jews. They spent their final day at Sachsenhausen, a nearby concentration camp that was built in 1936 and housed hundreds of thousands of prisoners until its liberation in 1945.

The trip marked a return for the men’s basketball program. In 2018, the team traveled to Auschwitz, guided through the camp by survivor Eva Mozes Kor. That trip was set in motion by Amanda Caleb '02, a former Davidson athlete who, with Gallin, facilitated this summer's program in Berlin as well. 

Davidson's experience in Berlin is now the model the Ferencz Institute is building on to bring immersive Holocaust education to collegiate athletes across the country, through its Athletes Against Antisemitism and Discrimination initiative. 

“It gave me a new perspective on everything,” sophomore forward Jackson Keith said. “My previous education on the Holocaust didn’t cover anything we covered here. Seeing everything here really makes me motivated to speak out.”

For more, the team posted reflections and photos during their trip on the The Ferencz Institute: Beyond the Game Substack.

item.title: Your Voice, Your Story: Davidson Senior Admission Fellows on How to Apply, Stand Out and Find Your Fit
item.description:
Your Voice, Your Story: Davidson Senior Admission Fellows on How to Apply, Stand Out and Find Your Fit brashton@david… Mon, 09/28/2026 - 09:51

My Davidson | A Student Blog Your Voice, Your Story: Davidson Senior Admission Fellows on How to Apply, Stand Out and Find Your Fit

1790596800

When you’re sitting in front of a blank Common Application screen, it’s easy to feel like you’re trying to solve a puzzle with no official answer key. What do admission counselors actually want to read? How do you write a "Why Davidson" essay that feels authentic? And who is supposed to write that unique peer recommendation? 

To help you cut through the noise, we went straight to the experts: Davidson College’s Senior Admission Fellows.

About the Authors

As current students who work daily inside the Office of Admission, these seniors don't just live the Davidson experience, they observe how applications are evaluated from the inside out. As adjunct staff members of Davidson’s Office of Admission and Financial Aid, these students help conduct information sessions and online “Chat with a Wildcat” sessions, they lead project areas including social media, visit programming and data analysis, and they take part in the recruitment and selection of new students.

 

Meet the 2026-2027 Senior Admission Fellows

Having recently navigated the process themselves, they've pulled together their top advice on essay topics, deadlines, campus visits and staying true to yourself in this process.

Ask questions!!! Whether it’s about classes, food, culture, clubs, anything that sparks your curiosity in the slightest. At Davidson, you’ll find it’s very difficult to find someone who doesn’t want to talk about their experience. Students, professors and alumni will happily tell you what challenged them, what surprised them, and what made this place feel like home. Show that you’re someone who’s eager to learn from others, listen deeply, and join a community built on connection. Curiosity isn’t something that’s just encouraged at Davidson; it’s a part of the culture.

Josephine Niu ’27

Raleigh, North Carolina

Meet Jo

Get started early and plan out your applications. Senior year is full of so many fun things, and you don’t want to miss out or stress about applications. Spend your summer before senior year narrowing down the list of schools you'd like to apply to, and find a way to organize the dates that they are due. That way there won’t be any jumpscare deadlines, and you will be able to submit thoughtful rather than rushed applications. You have lots to offer, so make sure that your applications reflect that!

Alex Marron ’27

Chicago, Illinois

Meet Alex

In all of your written materials, make sure you’re using your own voice to tell your own story. Don’t worry too much about trying to sound impressive, or like what you think an admission officer wants to hear. Instead, focus on communicating what makes you unique — your experiences, interests, personality, values, and the things you genuinely care about. The strongest applications feel authentic and give the reader a clear sense of who the student is beyond their grades and activities. The key to success in any admissions process isn’t trying to squeeze yourself into a particular box. It’s taking the time to understand what you’re looking for and finding the schools, programs, and communities where you’ll do well.

Will Capps '27

Cary, North Carolina

Meet Will

Keep in mind that this is a community where people want the best for you. Applying to college is stressful, and it is hard not to feel overwhelmed or like a cog in the machine. But the Davidson community is one that will be generous to you. The Admission team wants to see you in your best light and in your unique context, so remember to give them information that helps them do that. Use space like the Additional Information section or your essay responses to explain the why behind your path, whether that means sharing how family responsibilities shaped your schedule or detailing an academic obstacle you overcame. This is hard work you have done — trust your voice, be honest about your journey, and show them who you truly are. 

Mishti Mookherjee ’27

Bengaluru, India

Meet Mishti

Be true to yourself! Find the story that really shows who you are, what you want from Davidson, and how you can contribute to the community. When it came to writing college essays, I constantly heard that you should connect your story to something tangible. I didn’t believe it until I wrote my own essay, which began with the words, “I am a chair.” It sounds ridiculous, but I took that advice to heart and wrote about four stories (or four people) who have grounded me throughout my life and helped me balance myself, just like a chair balances on four legs. Never think your idea is ridiculous. Write it down, work with it and put your unique story to the test. That is one of the best things you can do when it comes to writing your essay!

Greg Coppola ’27

Glen Head, New York

Meet Greg

Talk to as many current students as you can! A History major, a violin player, a club tennis member — learn about aspects of college that interest you, but also involvements that may not initially be on your radar. In doing so, you’ll be able to paint the picture of what your own college experience may look like. Referencing specific classes, clubs, professors, and other experiences will make writing your “Why Davidson” so much easier, and will give you a sense of whether a school is the right fit for you. 

Maya Rajeh ’27

Hamilton, Bermuda

Meet Maya

When thinking about applying to Davidson, I didn’t know what to talk about. Sure, I volunteered in my community and engaged in student organizations in high school, but I didn’t know how to discuss my experiences. I spent a great deal of time trying to craft the perfect profile, and at a certain point, I began to see a disconnect between the person writing the application and the applicant I was writing about. However, my high school college advisor gave me valuable advice: no one expects an 18-year-old to have everything figured out. Nor do they expect an 18-year-old to have a complete mapping of their life. It’s great to have an idea, but Davidson wants to see you holistically, not just your aspirations supported by test scores and transcripts. Yes, those are factors, but they aren’t you. So the best advice I can give you is to be yourself, and to not shy away from what makes you an individual. Talk about your interests. Talk about your hobbies. Share your art. Talk about that niche topic you think no one cares about. It might not seem that interesting to you, but we aren’t looking for perfection; we are looking for people who would thrive in this community, and why not share?

Romeo Norris ’27

Huntingtown, Maryland

Meet Romeo

Find your why before you apply. I know it sounds cliché but if you yourself don’t know why Davidson, or any other school, is the best fit for you, then writing about that is going to be really challenging. Find something that makes you genuinely excited about Davidson. It can be small or seemingly silly, but if it is something you are really passionate about (coffee on campus, a study spot, a professor…), that will come through naturally in your writing.

Annalee Stuardi-Drumm ’27

Upper Darby, Pennsylvania

Meet Annalee

As a first-generation college student, asking questions was invaluable during my college search. Do not be afraid to reach out to current students, admission counselors, and staff with questions. At Davidson College, everyone is more than willing to answer any question you may have. Try to really get to know the schools you will be applying to through virtual/in-person tours, zoom/in-person panels with current students, or by emailing a current student, professor or admission counselor. You will be there for the next four years, so make sure the college you choose will fit both your personal and academic needs.

Priscila Plancarte ’27

Los Angeles/Santa Rosa, California

Meet Priscila

Find a great person for your peer recommendation. I chose one of my childhood best friends to write mine and I could not have picked a better person. Naturally with college recommendations, we want someone who makes us “look good,” whether that be in academics, service, or extracurriculars. However, Davidson is a community of real people — those who have amazing qualities but also room for personal growth. Choose someone who truly knows you — the good and the bad — and ask them early. The peer recommendation is a unique and special part of your application, so let it shine!

Ann Thompson ’27

Mount Pleasant, South Carolina

Meet Ann

Ready to start the application process?

Get Admission Process Help
Find information on testing, pre-college credit and other FAQs.

My Davidson | A Student Blog Davidson College Rock Band Fool’s Errand Records Debut EP

Fool's Errand in front of Tweed's front hallway sign: (left to right) Ezra Minard '28, Roan O'Reilly, Peter Diugu '27, Enzo Guardado '27, Annabel Semans '26, Jacob Kim '26, Jayson Rivera '27, Paige Pakenas '25, Nikola Cope '28. Henry Erickson '26 not pictured.

The popular Davidson College student rock band Fool’s Errand recently recorded their debut EP in Athens, Georgia. Learn how interdisciplinary collaboration, funding from the Jay Hurt Hub for Innovation and Entrepreneurship, and alumni mentorship brought their music from campus to the studio.

About the Author

Nikola Cope '28 (he/him) is a double major in economics and psychology from Athens, Georgia. On campus, he is involved with The Legacy Project and served as a student consultant at The Hurt Hub at Davidson College, our center for innovation and entrepreneurship. He is also a QuestBridge Scholar.

"I chose Davidson because of the possibilities it inspired me to imagine. Halfway through my time here, I can confidently say that Davidson holds a vast, New York-sized universe of possibilities within just 650 acres. I do what I do now to honor why Davidson picked someone like me: a student who was matched to this incredible school."

I love Davidson deeply, and I love my hometown just as much. 

At its core, my idea evolved from imagining how these two loves of mine could weave together. I first conceived of this project during my freshman year, when I set out to get the band into an Athens studio to record an album. After more than a year and a half of setbacks, I truly came to understand the Hurt Hub at Davidson’s motto: "Failure is Not Final." Through that journey, remarkable people from inside and outside the Davidson community made something incredible happen. 

I hope you'll read Ezra Minard's ('28) piece to learn about this journey; he's a real writer and my friend, and he tells this story far better than I could. Listen to our EP, Final Errand, too. Or do both at once, as any Davidson student would.

The Davidson community stretches out far beyond its campus like a rubber band pulled wider than necessary to only then snuggly pull people and ideas together in their most awesome configuration.

item.title: Interest Rates, Debt and the U.S. Outlook: Unpacking the Bond Yield Surge
item.description:
Interest Rates, Debt and the U.S. Outlook: Unpacking the Bond Yield Surge vabreese@david… Wed, 09/16/2026 - 16:20

Interest Rates, Debt and the U.S. Outlook: Unpacking the Bond Yield Surge

1789560000

Interest rates on U.S. government bonds have climbed to their highest levels in years, and the effects show up in mortgage rates, in car loans — in the cost of borrowing almost anything.

Davidson College Economics Professor Vikram Kumar 

The forces pushing them up are tangled — stubborn inflation, oil, tariffs, a new Federal Reserve chair and a national debt that keeps outgrowing the economy.

Vikram Kumar, professor of economics at Davidson College, says how you feel about the situation depends on where you sit.

"As a consumer, I worry a little bit,” he said. “As a saver, I'm on the happy side."

Here, he talks about what's pushing long-term interest rates higher, how the national debt figures in, and why he remains "generally bullish" about the U.S. economy.

What’s behind the spike in bond yields?

There's uncertainty about inflation, uncertainty about the course of monetary policy, uncertainty about supply chains, oil, tariffs, AI and national debt sustainability. Technically, both inflationary expectations and the term premium can be behind the spike in long-term interest rates.

It's an idiosyncratic confluence of factors buffeting the bond market today, which is what makes it very different from prior interest rate shocks. On the surface, it's another very rapid increase in interest rates, but behind it, the factors leading up to it are quite different from the past.

The national debt recently crossed $40 trillion; that’s up $17 trillion since 2020, and the CBO projects it will reach roughly $64 trillion within a decade. How does that affect the bond market?

When the government runs deficits, it borrows funds in the bond market by selling bonds. That lowers the price of bonds. Because bond prices and interest rates are inversely related, the interest rates rise. Stated differently, the government is competing with other borrowers for loanable funds. The more the government borrows, the greater the competition for funds — everybody has to pay a higher interest rate.

The bond market is unusually competitive at the moment. Part of the increase has been driven by an incredibly large issuance of private debt by companies like Meta that are hyperscalers in the AI world. They are investing trillions of dollars for data center buildouts, which is adding to the interest cost for the U.S. Treasury because the government is competing with those firms.

Interest rates are also likely signaling the bond market’s concern about the sustainability of a large and rising debt relative to our GDP — this concern rises when the interest rate exceeds the economic growth rate.

Is this a U.S. story or a global one?

It's a global issue now — sovereign debt issues have increased around the world. The United Kingdom, Japan and France have seen record increases in interest rates in the past month. It's a signal to policymakers and to politicians to fix their fiscal houses. 

Higher oil prices and inflationary expectations and anticipated central bank tightening have investors demanding larger term premiums for holding long-duration debt. The fiscal situation only amplifies their concerns.

Governments have three options to control the debt outlook: raise taxes, lower spending or increase the rate of growth so that they can afford to service the debt. The U.S. is fortunate to have higher growth than Europe right now, so we can increase our tax revenue base. 

How does this compare with past interest rate shocks?

Sudden large increases have happened before, but we are not as well positioned right now because of the size of the national debt. In the 1970s, interest rates went up a lot, but at that time inflationary expectations were getting unanchored. That is not a worry right now. Inflationary expectations are higher than optimal, but they are tethered. In the mid-1990s, the Fed increased rates very rapidly during the “Great Bond Massacre,” but then the national debt was much lower and inflation was not a factor. 

Interest rate shocks like this can have unintended consequences. In 2022, when the Fed increased interest rates very quickly to combat inflation, it had unforeseeable repercussions — ultimately resulting in the failure of Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank, for example. 

Are foreign investors backing away from U.S. debt? Is the dollar losing its status as the reserve currency?

There was a recent news item about the Norwegian sovereign wealth fund trying to move away from its dollar holdings. But on the whole, the inflow of foreign funds into Treasuries has been quite stable. The latest Treasury International Capital data for June showed healthy foreign inflows into Treasuries, from both private and public sources. Foreign holding of the national debt had declined significantly in the last decade, but for the last six years it has also been fairly stable. To me the data doesn't indicate reduced interest in U.S. dollar debt.

Of course, the U.S. has to be careful to not undermine its privilege or status as a reserve currency. The dollar's share in global foreign exchange holdings is pretty healthy and stable. I think the Dollar Buyers Club hasn't blackballed the dollar, though some members of that club are trying.

How are you feeling about the economy overall?

I'm generally bullish about the U.S. economy, cautiously so. I have reason to be if one looks at the data itself. The U.S. economy has been growing very well, and though the inflation rate is not ideal, the job market has not broken despite a lot of the challenges. The U.S. economy has defied the odds before.

That doesn't mean there aren't problems. Wage growth is not yet outpacing inflation, so people are not feeling very happy. On the other hand, asset markets are doing really well. How one feels depends upon where in the spectrum of the economy one sits. So I am not Pollyanna-ish about it. But the U.S. is an economy from which you can expect reasonably good outcomes.

item.title: Bacteria Making You Sick? Here's a Virus for You
item.description:
Bacteria Making You Sick? Here's a Virus for You brashton@david… Mon, 09/14/2026 - 13:03

Bacteria Making You Sick? Here's a Virus for You

1789387200

This summer, a team of seven students joined their professor on the front lines of the high-stakes battle between antibiotics and bacteria. 

Since the first dose of penicillin was administered in the 1940s, humans have been fighting to maintain antibiotics’ effectiveness. Bacteria evolve quickly, often developing resistance to the medications that have saved so many lives. If nothing changes, antibiotics will eventually lose their life-saving power. A 2024 study in The Lancet predicts that by 2050, almost two million people will die every year from drug-resistant infections, an increase of about 70% from 2021 levels.

Biology Professor Bryan Thurtle-Schmidt

“There are two things we can do about it,” Biology Professor Bryan Thurtle-Schmidt said. “We can try to preserve our most powerful antibiotics by not using them frequently. That way, bacteria don't have the opportunity to develop resistance.

“Or we can try to create new ones, which is hard. It can take at least 20 years for an R&D pipeline to develop a new drug.”

Thurtle-Schmidt’s team is working on a third way. Instead of developing a chemical that can kill bacteria, they (and a host of researchers across the world) hope to transform viruses into targeted weapons.

“If you get sick and there aren't antibiotics that will cure you, how great would it be if we have a cocktail of viruses that will search and destroy the bacteria that are making you sick?,” he said. “I think one day we could get there, but in the meantime, we need people, including the researchers in my lab, studying the interactions between viruses and bacteria.” 

It starts with a class of viruses called “phages.” Phages infect only bacteria; they present no infection threat to human cells. And when phages, which Thurtle-Schmidt said look like “alien robots,” inject their genetic material into bacteria, they mass-produce copies of themselves until they kill and break out of the bacteria.

Bacteria have developed defenses against phages and that resistance is the focus of Thurtle-Schmidt’s lab. Understanding the interaction between phages and the proteins in the bacteria membranes that fight them off is the key to turning the tide against bacteria. 

“I care a lot about the structure of these molecules because the thing we say in biology all the time is that ‘structure determines function.’ The more we understand about what a molecule looks like, the more we can rationalize what it does,” Thurtle-Schmidt said.

The "Summer Squad" Whiteboard

His research is promising enough that the National Institutes of Health awarded him a three-year, $400,790 grant in 2024.  

The seven students — they called themselves the “Summer Squad” — worked in Thurtle-Schmidt’s lab on the third floor of the E. Craig Wall Jr. Academic Center. They covered a whiteboard in the corner with photos of each student clutching a plush prairie dog. (The stuffed animals are gifts from the lab supply company for frequent customers, like Thurtle-Schmidt, and they have become the unofficial mascot of his lab.)

The students came for different reasons — a career they could already see, or a corner of biology they wanted to try out.

“There are a lot of implications down the road with this research,” said junior Sahaana Rajagopalan, who plans to attend medical school to become a physician.

“This therapy could be used to combat this never-ending arms race,” she said. “I'll be able to use this with my future profession.”

“I know that I want to study biology, but I've really been trying to explore what it is within biology, and the field of cell and molecular biology specifically, that I enjoy doing,” Kian Sarkar ’28 said. “This is more directly working with the kinds of things that are involved in the mechanisms of infection and pathogenesis.”

The students split into two teams, each taking one side of the same problem. One group asked what the bacteria's defense proteins actually do, purifying them and testing their activity in the lab. The other asked whether candidate genes actually provide defense for the bacteria against phages, switching them on in E. coli and turning a collection of viruses loose.

Rebecca Polgar is a junior biology major with a Hispanic Studies minor who spent her summer focused on the bacteria’s viral defenses. Polgar is studying in Panama this fall but, like most of her fellow researchers, she hopes to return to the lab in the spring. 

“I work on a specific type of protein to mechanistically say, ‘Okay, this is how the protein is in charge of defending the bacteria against the phages,’” Polgar said. “The way it defends against phages in the cell is by cleaving or cutting the phage DNA. So how does the salt concentration of the solution the bacteria and phages are in affect how my protein cuts DNA?”

“When you're cooking in the kitchen and you’re like, ‘Wow, that meal was really good. What was the secret ingredient?’ It might be the cumin, or, it might be the salt,” Polgar said. “But, in the lab, just like any meal, it's the combination of ingredients and how they interact with each other.”

By August, Polgar and her colleagues had developed a few of the ingredients.

Valentina Cova ’28 produced one of the summer's most striking results: her research hints at how a cell senses an incoming virus and triggers a defensive reaction. Polgar and Rajagopalan came at the same pair of genes from opposite directions, biochemical and genetic, and their findings fit together. Reyna Mehta ’29 showed that a protein the lab had only studied genetically can cut DNA. Gabrielle Shelton ’28 confirmed that a poorly understood gene provides defense; Charlie Price ’29 confirmed that a new, previously uncharacterized gene did not defend against viruses. Sarkar built software to hunt phage genomes for proteins that disable those defenses.

Members of the Summer Squad will present their findings at the Summer Research Symposium at 7 p.m. on Tuesday, Sept. 15 in the Alvarez College Union.

The summer changed how the students see themselves. 

“On the first day, I was scared to use the autoclave because it looked like this big machine. I was so overwhelmed,” Rajagopalan said. “But now I feel like all those things are second nature.”

Their technical skills have grown but they’ve also learned about the challenges of research. 

“Things might not always work out and things take time,” Rajagopalan said. “I've run so many experiments, and I've had to repeat things and change things, and I think that, in general, the persistence I’ve learned will be super-important because medical school is a long road.” 

They’ve also grown together: “I didn't know many of my fellow researchers coming into the lab,” Sarkar said. “But now I have made several great friends. You get to meet a lot of new people and gain valuable experience.”

“This summer was like diving into the deep end,” Polgar said. “I was wondering, ‘Do I like research? Is this what I want to do for the rest of my life?’ And it turns out that yes, it is. I've been falling in love with research, which is so cheesy, but it's true. Bryan has my dream job.”

item.title: An Ache to be Back: Keith Kleeman ’97 Returns to Davidson as Alumni Innovator-in-Residence
item.description:
An Ache to be Back: Keith Kleeman ’97 Returns to Davidson as Alumni Innovator-in-Residence vabreese@david… Thu, 09/03/2026 - 08:38

An Ache to be Back: Keith Kleeman ’97 Returns to Davidson as Alumni Innovator-in-Residence

1788436800

For Keith Kleeman ’97, joining Davidson College as the new Alumni Innovator-in-Residence at the Jay Hurt Hub for Innovation & Entrepreneurship isn’t just a new role — it’s the ultimate homecoming. 

Keith Kleeman ’97 

During his 1997 commencement address, President Emeritus John Kuykendall ’59 explained to Kleeman and his classmates that nostalgia is an “ache to be back in a place.” Kleeman had never considered the deeper meaning of the word, and hearing it defined that way struck something in him that has endured for nearly three decades.

Through the Peace Corps, graduate school, building companies and a career that took him far from Davidson, the words stayed with him. 

“I remember hearing Dr. Kuykendall explain what nostalgia really meant, and it just hit me that afternoon,” Kleeman said. “An ache to be back in a place. To return to this place. I had never thought about the word that way. I still have the original program that contains a copy of his speech, and it sits on my desk today. I don’t think I could have known at 21 how much those words would eventually mean to me.”

Decades after hearing those words and earning his diploma, the serial biotechnology entrepreneur is making his long-awaited return, bringing a wealth of experience back to the community that shaped him.

The Unconventional Path

Recruited for the men’s soccer team, Kleeman arrived at Davidson with support from athletic scholarships, grants and the Bonner Scholars Program.

His path through college quickly proved less conventional.

“I never fit neatly into one academic box,” Kleeman said. “I loved science, but I also loved literature and writing. At the time, those interests seemed unrelated. It turned out that learning to live in both worlds was one of the most valuable things Davidson gave me.”

Kleeman began as a biology major but found himself increasingly drawn to reading, writing and the outdoors. Without the time to change majors and still graduate on schedule, he completed his biology degree while writing a novel on the side. Professor Emeritus Bill Mahoney took on the novel as a senior project, while former Bonner Scholars Program Director Ruth Pittard and the late Head Men’s Soccer Coach Charlie Slagle provided the mentorship — and occasional tough love — that helped him rebound from a difficult first semester.

By graduation, what had once seemed like disconnected interests had become an education that crossed traditional boundaries between the sciences and humanities.

The Hurt Hub is Davidson College's home for innovation and entrepreneurship, open to students, alumni, faculty, staff, entrepreneurs and the Greater Charlotte community.

“It’s the constellation of components that makes Davidson so special — the faculty, the students, the academic rigor and the overall culture of acceptance and welcome,” Kleeman said. “If it were just one of those things, it would be easy to reproduce. Academic rigor by itself isn’t unique; there are plenty of places that have that. There are very few places that bring all of those things together the way Davidson does.”

At 21, diploma in hand, Kleeman was ready to see where that education might take him. After a disappointing near-miss for a Watson Fellowship, he joined the Peace Corps and spent two years working in coastal resource management in the Philippines. The experience fundamentally changed how he thought about opportunity, service and success.

“In America, a lot of times, the first thing people want to know about you is what you do for a living. In the Philippines, people don’t define themselves that way,” Kleeman said. “Living there made me think first about the opportunities I have and how those opportunities allow me to make someone else’s life better. I learned that if doing good isn’t your primary focus, you’ve missed the point. If you do good first, success follows, and it’s that kind of success you can feel great about.”

From there would come graduate school, medical writing, entrepreneurship, artificial intelligence and biotechnology. Kleeman would build companies, help bring new medicines through the regulatory process and spend much of his career solving problems at the intersection of science, technology and human health.

Along the way, the unconventional combination he had begun assembling at Davidson — science and literature, analytical thinking and storytelling, ambition and service — became not a collection of unrelated interests, but one of the defining strengths of his career.

And through it all, he remained nostalgic for Davidson.

From Medical Writing to AI and Biotech

Kleeman eventually combined a Davidson biology degree, his Peace Corps experience and a master’s degree in English literature from Xavier University in a way that would have been difficult to predict when he was an undergraduate: medical writing at Eli Lilly and Company.

That work led him to launch his first venture, Medical Communication Consultants (MCC), and began more than two decades of building companies at the intersection of science, writing and technology.

He founded MCC and scaled it to 400 writers, supporting the regulatory approval of more than 25 therapeutics. He later created ClinGenuity, which developed one of the pharmaceutical industry’s earliest artificial intelligence platforms using natural language recognition and processing to automate the creation of regulatory documents.

Following the combination of MCC and ClinGenuity and their acquisition by Certara, Kleeman served as vice president of strategy and clinical innovation. Today, he is founder and CEO of Celvant and Optimvia, companies advancing synthetic heparin and platforms designed to modernize drug manufacturing.

The career that followed Davidson, in other words, ended up looking remarkably like the education he received there: science mixed with writing, technology with creativity, ambition with service.

Nearly 30 years after graduation, Kleeman is returning to the place where those pieces first came together as the Alumni Innovator-in-Residence for the Hurt Hub to help a new generation of Wildcats discover where their own unexpected combinations might take them.

Redefining Innovation at the Hurt Hub

As the Alumni Innovator-in-Residence, Kleeman wants to demystify entrepreneurship for current Davidson students and help them see innovation as something much broader — and more accessible — than founding a company.

Innovation has nothing to do with starting a business. Being an innovator isn’t some mysterious quality you’re born with. It’s a way of approaching the world. Innovators see problems and obstacles as opportunities — their instinct is not to be discouraged by what isn’t working, but to ask, ‘How do I fix this?’ That’s the mindset shift. You don’t have to build a company or invent the next big thing to be an innovator. You need the curiosity to see what could be better, the confidence to try something different and the tools to turn an idea into action. Will that always result in a successful business? No. That’s not the point. Innovation is about how you approach problems in the first place.

Alumni Innovator-in-Residence Keith Kleeman ’97

He also wants students to understand something his own career has repeatedly reinforced: the people they choose to surround themselves with may matter as much as any individual idea.

“I’ve been very lucky in terms of selecting really good people to be around who care about what happens to me and who also happen to be incredibly smart and accomplished,” he said. “I want students to understand how choosing the right mentors and partners can pay dividends for decades.”

At the Hurt Hub, Kleeman plans to hold open office hours, mentor student startups and help students bridge the distance between an interesting idea and meaningful real-world impact. Just as importantly, he hopes students who do not think of themselves as entrepreneurs will walk through the door.

For someone whose own Davidson experience resisted easy categorization, that may be particularly fitting.

The Ache to Be Back

Kleeman’s return comes with another full-circle moment. His youngest daughter, Annie, is joining Davidson’s Class of 2030 as a women’s soccer scholar-athlete — arriving on the same campus where her father first came as a recruited soccer player nearly three decades earlier.

And so a word from Commencement in 1997 has acquired a meaning Kleeman could not have understood when he first heard it.

Nostalgia: an ache to be back in a place.

After Davidson came the Peace Corps, graduate school, companies, medicines, artificial intelligence, biotechnology and a career built around turning ideas into things that might make a difference.

But the place kept pulling.

Now, nearly three decades later, Kleeman is back — not to recreate his Davidson experience, but to help students create their own.

item.title: Class of 2030 Dons Festive Duds, Dodges Downpour for Cake Race
item.description:
Class of 2030 Dons Festive Duds, Dodges Downpour for Cake Race brashton@david… Fri, 08/28/2026 - 08:45

Class of 2030 Dons Festive Duds, Dodges Downpour for Cake Race

1787918400

It’s a safe bet that Odysseus’s Trojan Horse didn’t taste like chocolate.

And that it wasn’t surrounded by Teddy Graham soldiers.

Then again, ancient Troy bears little resemblance to modern Davidson, but a clever baker tapped into the summer’s blockbuster film The Odyssey and turned it into a confection if not worth dying for, certainly desirable enough to run for on a hot muggy day. 

Ambitious concoctions didn’t stop there. There was a gorgeous My Little Pony cake; some Minions, and various treats bearing the number 30 in honor of NBA legend Stephen Curry ’10.

They’re among the many creations that inspired first-year students running in Davidson College’s annual Cake Race on Wednesday. Runners put their own spin on things, with costumes ranging from a banana to glamorous cats to a winning Christmas tree. 

Despite the downpour just before the race started, the college community turned out in a big way to cheer the runners on.

It’s Tradition

And now, for a little history.

This cherished tradition started in 1930 when an enterprising track coach wanted to see how much new talent he could recruit by using cake to lure first-year students to compete in a race.

They didn’t have much choice; the college made it mandatory for the students, then all male, to run the race. Today, it’s optional, but still very popular.

Then, faculty members’ wives made the cakes. Today, donations range from elaborate cakes, cupcakes and cookies crafted by everyone from nearby elementary school students to faculty, staff, neighbors, alumni and local businesses. Parents also get into the act, with some from far away sending local bakery cakes in honor of their runners. 

Men and women race separately. Winners normally come from the college’s track and field teams; but others who don’t usually run competitively also claim some impressive finishes — and cakes.

Track and field runners led the race again this year.

Dressed as a Christmas tree, festive phenom Eric Robinson III, from Evans, Georgia, won the men’s race, seeming to glide effortlessly in ahead of the pack. He chose a lovely cake titled “Mr. Duck Is Superb” as his bounty. 

With cat ears on her head and whiskers on her face, Amelia Lapierre, from Tucson, Arizona, won the women’s race and chose the “My Little Pony” cake.

Men’s Tennis Coach Drew Barrett, always a feted Cake Race baker, crafted the pony with his older daughter, Kennedy, while his younger daughter, Xie, took honors for the duck. Barrett’s wife, Mandy, assisted on both cakes.

The fun continued well after the competition.

Many students swear by Cake Race night, where runners share their abundance with hallmates and teammates. Students roam dorm floors on a cake-hopping mission, stopping to socialize and sample the goods.

It’s quintessential Davidson, and one of many ways the community shows its newcomers that they’re welcomed, supported and surrounded by caring people who want them to have a great college experience. 

On Wednesday afternoon, Katie Herbert trekked into the Baker Sports Complex with her young kids balancing large cakes in small hands. Liam, 5, carried a strawberry lemonade cake while Emma Kate, 3, proudly displayed her coconut cake.

The family recently moved to Davidson from Colorado and learned about the race at Liam’s new school, Davidson Elementary, where he started kindergarten this week. The kids looked longingly at the multitude of cakes displayed on tables; their mom held their hands to ensure they didn’t touch any.

Liam, already a sports fan, was equally awestruck by the athletic complex. He looks forward to Davidson baseball, basketball, volleyball and any other games.

Herbert loves that their new town is so closely connected to the college and says they’ll visit often.

“I heard about the Cake Race and thought it was a really great tradition and wanted to contribute something,” she said. “We’re happy to support the students.”

Liam reinforced that message:

“We want to support the students,” he said. “And come to a lot of baseball games.”

item.title: Davidson College Gathers 24 Colleges and Universities to Launch National Deliberative Citizenship Network
item.description:
Davidson College Gathers 24 Colleges and Universities to Launch National Deliberative Citizenship Network bewilliams1@da… Mon, 08/24/2026 - 13:11

Davidson College Gathers 24 Colleges and Universities to Launch National Deliberative Citizenship Network

1787572800

Professors from two dozen higher education institutions gathered at Davidson College last week to help their home campuses do something that’s become less common across the country: talk about topics that usually end conversations.

They belonged to the first cohort of the Deliberative Citizenship Network, a new national initiative led by Davidson and funded by a $4 million grant from the U.S. Department of Education. The network will operate out of Davidson’s D.G. and Harriet Wall Martin Institute for Public Good. Over the next four years, the DCN will expand to as many as 100 colleges and universities working to strengthen civil discourse, civic learning and democratic engagement on their campuses.

The group spanned the nation and higher education, from major research universities, such as the University of Pittsburgh and the University of Arkansas, to historically Black Delaware State University and Maryland’s Carroll Community College. Small liberal arts colleges, such as Washington and Lee, are working alongside large private universities, such as Tufts and DePaul.

Their classrooms differ in size and student profile but present the same challenge: helping college students learn to engage with one another in an era of polarization and fragmentation.

Prof. Graham Bullock

“In a society of people of many backgrounds and beliefs, it seems far easier to reinforce divisions instead of building areas of shared agreement,” Davidson President Doug Hicks ’90 said in his opening remarks. “The Deliberative Citizenship Network is bringing faculty members and colleges and universities together to help students develop capacities to contribute to the public good.” 

Graham Bullock organized and facilitated the two-day deliberative pedagogy workshop with support from several new grant-funded staff members. Bullock is a political science professor and founding director of the Deliberative Citizenship Initiative (DCI), on which the national network is based. Bullock has led the DCI at Davidson over the past six years and wrote the application that secured the federal grant for the network.

The sessions at Davidson aimed to help professors integrate deliberation into their courses so students can verbally and productively wrestle with challenging material and contentious topics. Deliberative  teaching methods help students deepen their understanding of course topics by listening curiously, speaking candidly, weighing competing arguments and evidence, and reasoning through difficult questions with others.

Early on the first day, Bullock split the faculty into small groups, each assigned to adopt and defend a different model of deliberation — deliberation as philosophical argument, participatory decision-making, psychological process or pedagogical approach — before reorganizing into mixed groups for rapid-fire rounds of disagreement. The exercise was designed to help faculty both examine the different models and learn how to design a real exchange of ideas in the few minutes that even a packed syllabus can include.

“Building courses around meaningful disagreement can enliven learning and allow faculty to pull public issues into the classroom,” Bullock told the attendees. “It also encourages students to use these skills in their lives — modeling the listening, the ethical arguments and reasoning that empowers them to be engaged citizens after they graduate.”

Those skills are exactly what drew Sarah Star, a philosophy and humanities professor at Carroll Community College, to the DCN.

“My students are anxious. They’re hesitant to embrace their roles in society,” she said. “My main goal is to prepare them to be citizens. I want to help them think about who they are, what they value and where they can contribute to leaving the world a better place than they found it.

“I’m hopeful the DCN framework will help them better understand the systems of citizenship and learn how to more effectively communicate with one another.”

These conversations aren't confined to classes that touch on the obviously political. Some of the hardest ones show up in fields so technical that most people can't even follow the disagreement, let alone take a side. 

“There’s still a lot we don’t understand about quantum mechanics,” said Heidi Hendrickson, a chemistry professor at Pennsylvania’s Lafayette College. “And it turns out many physicists disagree about how we describe the quantum world at a philosophical level.”

 She plans to incorporate deliberation into her first-year seminar: “Quantum Revolutions, Past and Present.” 

“Students can come in with the notion that scientific theories are more like doctrines,” she said. “But we are still figuring out the science. We are on the cusp of a scientific revolution, and I want students to realize they have the capability to make the next big discovery.”

The workshop was just the beginning. The faculty in the room will continue learning together through the year ahead, meeting virtually and sharing lessons learned as they take the new techniques home. As the DCN grows toward its goal of 100 campuses, this first cohort will adapt the model that Bullock and the DCI have pioneered to their own campuses, helping extend civil discourse at colleges across the country.
